summary: How AI tools create text, images, audio and video, how to write good prompts and check the results, and how to use generative AI honestly, safely and well.

intro: Generative AI can write an essay, paint a picture or clone a voice in seconds. In this topic you find out how it works, practise prompting it well, learn to check what it gives you, and think hard about how it is changing work, learning and the planet.

pages.title: What is generative AI?
pages.spec: Explain what generative AI is and give examples of what it can create
pages.summary: Generative AI is artificial intelligence that creates new content (text, images, audio, video or code) after learning patterns from huge amounts of examples. It is different from AI that only sorts or predicts.
pages.starter: Name three things a computer can make for you today that it could not make ten years ago.
sc: I can explain what makes AI "generative"
I can give examples of text, image, audio and video generators
I can explain the difference between generative AI and other AI

b: Most AI you meet sorts or predicts: is this email spam? which video next?
Generative AI creates something new: a story, a picture, a song, some code
It learns patterns from millions of examples, then makes new content that fits those patterns
You ask it with a prompt: an instruction typed or spoken in everyday language
slides.n: Show one quick live example on the board using the school-approved AI tool, e.g. ask for a four-line poem about Enniskillen. Ask: did it copy that poem from somewhere?

b: Text: chatbots and writing assistants answer questions, summarise and draft
Images: describe a picture and it draws it in any style
Audio: speech in someone's voice, music in any genre
Video: short clips from a description, or edits to real footage
Code: whole programs from a description (lesson 2 of "Coding with an AI assistant")
Training data: huge collections of text, images and sounds, much of it from the internet
The model is the result of training: a giant set of numbers that captures patterns
It does not store a copy of every example: it learns what usually goes together
More data and more computing power have made today's models far more capable
slides.n: Use the analogy of learning to cook by eating thousands of meals: you don't keep the meals, you learn what goes together.

blocks.text: Two kinds of AI

Most of the **[[artificial intelligence]]** you use every day is about **sorting and predicting**: your email app decides whether a message is spam, a streaming app predicts what you will watch next and your phone recognises your face. **[[Generative AI]]** is different: it **creates new content** that did not exist before.

blocks.caption: Sorting AI and generative AI
head: What it does
Example
Output
rows: Spam filter, face unlock, music recommendations
A label or a choice: "spam", "it's you", "play this next"
New text, pictures, sound, video or code

blocks.text: How does it learn?

A generative AI system is trained on enormous amounts of **[[training data]]**: billions of sentences, pictures or recordings. During training the computer adjusts millions (or billions) of numbers until it is very good at spotting patterns, for example which words usually follow others, or what a "cat" tends to look like. The finished set of numbers is called the **[[model]]**.
A model does not keep a copy of all its training data. It learns patterns, a bit like how you can draw a dog without tracing one, because you've seen thousands of dogs.
Asking it to make something

You control generative AI with a **[[prompt]]**: an instruction in everyday language, such as "Write a short ghost story set in a school computer room". The model uses the patterns it learned to produce something new that fits your prompt. Ask again and you will usually get a **different** answer, because the model picks from many likely options.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Generative AI creates new text, images, audio, video or code
It learns patterns from huge amounts of training data
The trained model is a big set of numbers, not a copy of the data
You tell it what to make with a prompt

blocks.title: Sort or create?
steps: Read the list of ten everyday AI uses your teacher shows on the board.
Decide for each one: does the AI sort/predict, or does it create something new?
Write your answers in the box, then compare with another pair.

q.q: List the uses you decided were generative AI.
q.a: Generative: writing an essay draft, making a picture from a description, creating a song, a voice assistant reading a story in a cloned voice, writing code. Sorting/predicting: spam filter, face unlock, film recommendations, predictive text choosing the next word to suggest, sat-nav traffic predictions.

q.q: Pick one example you disagreed about. Why was it tricky?
q.a: Predictive text is tricky: it predicts the next word (sorting/predicting) but chatbots use the same idea to generate whole answers, so the line between the two can blur.

check.q: What makes AI "generative"?
o: It creates new content such as text or images
It searches the internet for answers
check.why: Generative AI makes new content rather than just labelling or choosing.

check.q: Which of these is an example of generative AI?
o: An app that draws a picture from a description
check.why: Making a new picture is generating content.

check.q: What is training data?
o: The instructions you type into a chatbot
The answer the AI gives you
The computer the AI runs on
The examples an AI learns patterns from
check.why: Models learn from huge collections of examples called training data.

check.q: What do we call the instruction you give to a generative AI tool?
check.why: A prompt is the instruction, usually in everyday language.

practice.q: Explain the difference between generative AI and AI that sorts or predicts. Give an example of each.
practice.a: Generative AI creates new content (1), e.g. a chatbot writing a story or an image generator (1); other AI sorts or predicts, e.g. a spam filter or face unlock (1). Max 2.

practice.q: Explain why asking a generative AI tool the same prompt twice can give different answers.
practice.a: The model chooses from many likely options/words each time (1), so it doesn't always pick the same ones, so the output varies (1).

pages.title: How chatbots write
pages.spec: Describe how a large language model writes by predicting the next word
pages.summary: Chatbots are powered by large language models. They break text into tokens and write one token at a time, each time predicting what is most likely to come next based on the patterns they learned.
pages.starter: Finish the sentence: "Once upon a ..." How did you know what word comes next?
sc: I can explain what a large language model (LLM) is
I can describe how an LLM writes one token at a time
I can explain why fluent writing is not the same as being right

b: "Once upon a ..." you already know the answer: time
You learned that pattern from hearing thousands of stories
A large language model (LLM) does the same with billions of sentences
It writes by predicting the next small chunk of text, over and over
slides.n: Play "next word" round the class: start a sentence and each pupil adds one word. Point out that this is roughly how an LLM builds an answer.

b: Text is broken into tokens: whole words or pieces of words
"unbelievable" might be split into "un", "believ", "able"
The model gives every possible next token a probability
It picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats until the answer is finished

slides.t: Fluent is not the same as true
b: The model is choosing likely words, not checking facts
So it can sound confident and still be wrong
It can also be "creative" on purpose: a setting called temperature adds variety
Good users check important facts somewhere reliable
slides.n: Link forward to lesson 4 on hallucinations.

blocks.text: What is a large language model?

A **[[chatbot]]** such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot or Claude is powered by a **[[large language model]]** (**LLM**). An LLM is a generative AI model trained on a vast amount of text: books, websites, articles and conversations. From all that text it has learned which words tend to follow which, in which situations.
One token at a time

An LLM doesn't write a whole answer at once. It works in small chunks called **[[token|tokens]]**: whole words or parts of words. For every step it calculates how likely each possible next token is, picks one, adds it to the text, then predicts the next one, again and again.

blocks.title: Predicting the next token
blocks.context: The model has written: "The capital of France is"
steps: It scores every possible next token: "Paris" very likely, "a" less likely, "banana" almost impossible.
It picks "Paris" and adds it: "The capital of France is Paris".
It predicts again: "." is now very likely, so it adds a full stop and the answer is done.
blocks.answer: The answer is built by repeatedly choosing a likely next token, not by looking the fact up.

blocks.text: Why it can be wrong

Because an LLM chooses **likely** words rather than checking facts, it can write something that sounds perfect but is untrue. It can also mix up details when its training data had few examples of a topic. That is why you should treat a chatbot like a very well-read friend who sometimes makes things up: helpful, but worth checking.
Sounding confident does not mean being correct. A chatbot will rarely say "I'm not sure" unless it has been designed to.

blocks.title: Be the language model
steps: Your teacher gives each group a sentence starter and a bag of word cards.
Take turns to choose the most likely next word card and add it to the sentence.
After five words, choose one card that is unlikely but still makes sense. How does the sentence change?
Write your two sentences below.

q.q: Write your "most likely" sentence and your "surprising" sentence.
q.a: For example: "The school bus was late because of the snow." and "The school bus was late because of the dragon." Choosing less likely words makes the text more creative but less sensible.

q.q: Explain how this game is like the way an LLM writes.
q.a: An LLM also adds one token at a time, choosing from likely options based on patterns it has learned; sometimes it picks a less likely option, which adds variety but can lead to nonsense or mistakes.

check.q: What does LLM stand for?
check.why: An LLM is a large language model.

check.q: How does an LLM write an answer?
o: By asking a human to type it
By looking it up in a dictionary
By predicting the next token again and again
By copying a full answer from a website
check.why: It builds the answer one predicted token at a time.

check.q: What is a token?
o: A coin used to pay for AI
A word or part of a word that the model works with
check.why: Text is split into tokens: words or pieces of words.

check.q: Why can a chatbot give a wrong answer that sounds right?
o: It picks likely words rather than checking facts
check.why: Fluent text comes from patterns, not fact-checking.

practice.q: Describe how a large language model produces an answer to a question.
practice.a: Text is split into tokens (1); the model predicts the probability of each possible next token using patterns from training (1); it picks one, adds it and repeats until the answer is complete (1).

practice.q: Explain why you should check facts that a chatbot gives you.
practice.a: It predicts likely words and doesn't check facts (1), so it can produce answers that sound right but are wrong (1).

pages.title: Prompting well
pages.spec: Write clear prompts and improve them step by step to get better results
pages.summary: The quality of what generative AI gives you depends on the prompt. Good prompts give context, a clear task, a format and any limits, and you improve results by refining the prompt and asking follow-up questions.
pages.starter: Ask a friend to draw "an animal". Then ask for "a grumpy orange cat wearing a tiny hat, cartoon style". Which drawing will be closer to what you wanted?
sc: I can explain why vague prompts give poor results
I can use a prompt recipe: role, task, context, format, limits
I can improve a prompt by refining it

b: "Tell me about volcanoes" could mean anything
The AI has to guess your age, purpose and how much you want
Better prompts remove the guessing
Writing good prompts is called prompt engineering
Role: "You are a geography teacher for 12-year-olds"
Task: "Explain how volcanoes form"
Context: "for a revision page; we've learned about tectonic plates"
Format: "in 5 bullet points with one key word in bold each"
Limits: "under 120 words; use simple language"
slides.n: Write the five parts on the board and build a prompt live with the class.

b: Read the answer critically: is it what you need?
Refine: add detail, ask for a change, give an example
Follow up: "Make point 3 simpler" or "Give me a real example"
This loop of trying and improving is called iteration

blocks.text: Why prompts matter

A generative AI tool only knows what you tell it. A vague **[[prompt]]** such as "write about volcanoes" forces it to guess who you are and what you want. The skill of writing prompts that get useful results is called **[[prompt engineering]]**.
A prompt recipe

blocks.caption: Five parts of a good prompt
head: Part
What it does
Example
rows: Tells the AI who to act as
You are a friendly science teacher
For a Year 9 revision page; we know about tectonic plates
Says how to lay it out
Five bullet points, one key word in bold in each
Under 120 words, simple language, no jokes

blocks.text: You won't always need all five parts, but adding **[[context]]** and a **format** almost always helps.
Improve it: iteration

Your first prompt is rarely perfect. Read the answer carefully, then **refine** it: "make it shorter", "use an example from sport", "explain point 2 more simply". This cycle of trying, checking and improving is called **[[iteration]]**, the same idea programmers use when they test and improve code.
Never put personal information (your full name, address, school login or photos of people) into a prompt. Many AI tools keep what you type and may use it to improve their models.

blocks.title: Prompt makeover
steps: Use your school-approved AI tool (or the printed answers your teacher shows if you can't use one).
Type the vague prompt: "Write about the water cycle."
Rewrite it using the recipe: role, task, context, format and limits. Try it.
Refine it once more with a follow-up instruction.

q.a: Example: "You are a friendly geography teacher. Explain the water cycle to a 12-year-old for a revision card. Use four numbered steps (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection) with one sentence each, and finish with one quick question to test me. Under 100 words."

q.q: How was the second answer better than the first?
q.a: It matched my age and purpose, was the right length, was laid out the way I needed (numbered steps), and included a test question, so I didn't have to edit it as much.

check.q: Why does a vague prompt often give a poor answer?
o: The AI has to guess what you want
The AI only answers questions in capitals
check.why: Without detail, the AI guesses your age, purpose and format.

check.q: Which part of a prompt says how the answer should be laid out?
check.why: Format is about layout, e.g. bullet points or a table.

check.q: What is iteration when prompting?
o: Turning the AI off and on
Asking the same thing in capitals
Trying, checking and improving the prompt
check.why: Iteration means improving the prompt in cycles.

check.q: Which of these should you never put into a prompt?
check.why: Personal information can be stored by the AI tool.

practice.q: Rewrite this prompt to make it better, and explain one improvement: "Make a quiz."
practice.a: Any improved prompt with detail, e.g. "Make a 5-question multiple-choice quiz on the water cycle for 12-year-olds, with 4 options each and the answers at the end" (2); explanation, e.g. giving the topic/age/format means the AI doesn't have to guess (1).

practice.q: Give two reasons why you should not put personal information into an AI tool.
practice.a: Any two: it may be stored by the company (1); it may be used to train the model (1); it could be seen by others/leaked (1); it breaks school rules/privacy (1).

pages.title: Hallucinations and bias
pages.spec: Explain why generative AI makes mistakes and shows bias, and check its output
pages.summary: Generative AI can "hallucinate", inventing facts, quotes or sources, and it can repeat biases found in its training data. Good users verify important information with reliable sources and look for missing viewpoints.
pages.starter: A chatbot says "Enniskillen Castle was built in 1066 by William the Conqueror." How could you check whether that's true?
sc: I can explain what an AI hallucination is
I can explain how bias gets into an AI model
I can check AI output using reliable sources

b: A hallucination is when AI states something false as if it were true
It can invent facts, dates, quotes, people and even sources or web links
It happens because the model predicts likely words, not true ones
Hallucinations look exactly as confident as correct answers
slides.n: The starter example is invented. Enniskillen Castle dates from the 15th century (Maguire chieftains) and William the Conqueror never came to Ireland. A great example of plausible nonsense.

b: Training data comes from people, so it carries people's biases
If most pictures of "a scientist" in the data are men, the AI may draw mostly men
Some languages, cultures and places are under-represented
Bias can be unfair, hurtful or simply wrong
Is it important? The more it matters, the more you check
Cross-check facts with two reliable sources (BBC Bitesize, gov.uk, textbooks)
Click any links: do they exist and say what the AI claims?
Ask: whose view is missing?

blocks.text: AI hallucinations

An AI **[[hallucination]]** is when a generative AI tool produces information that is false but presents it as fact. It might invent a date, a quote from a famous person, a book that doesn't exist or a web link that leads nowhere. Hallucinations happen because the model is predicting **likely** words, not looking facts up, and they sound just as confident as correct answers.

blocks.title: Spotting a hallucination
blocks.context: A chatbot writes: "Enniskillen Castle was built in 1066 by William the Conqueror."
steps: Ask: does it sound plausible? Castles are old, and 1066 is a famous date, so it sounds believable.
Check a reliable source: the castle's own museum website and local history books say it was built in the 15th century by the Maguires.
Notice the trick: the AI joined two "castle-ish" facts (1066, William the Conqueror) that have nothing to do with Enniskillen.
blocks.answer: It's a hallucination: confident, plausible and wrong. Always verify facts that matter.

blocks.text: Bias

**[[bias|Bias]]** is when an AI system treats some people or ideas unfairly or one-sidedly. It usually comes from the training data: if the data contains more examples of some groups than others, or contains stereotypes, the model learns those patterns too. For example, an image generator asked for "a nurse" might mostly draw women, and one asked for "a CEO" might mostly draw men.
How to verify
To **[[verify]]** means to check that something is true. The more important the information, the more carefully you should check it.

items: Ask the tool for its sources, then open them: do they exist and say the same thing?
Cross-check with two reliable sources, such as BBC Bitesize, a textbook or an official website.
Look for missing viewpoints: who might see this differently?
If it's about a person, be extra careful: false information can hurt real people.

blocks.title: Fact-check the chatbot
steps: Your teacher shows five statements written by an AI chatbot about Northern Ireland.
For each one, use two reliable websites to decide: true, false or partly true.
Record the sources you used.

q.q: Which statements were hallucinations, and what was actually true?
q.a: Answers depend on the statements used, e.g. "The Giant's Causeway was built by the Romans" is false: it was formed by volcanic activity around 50-60 million years ago.

q.q: Which sources did you trust, and why?
q.a: Reliable sources are official, expert or well-known for checking facts (e.g. National Trust, BBC, a museum website), are up to date and agree with each other.

check.q: What is an AI hallucination?
o: When AI states something false as if it were true
When AI asks you a question
check.why: Hallucinations are confident but false outputs.

check.q: Where does bias in AI usually come from?
check.why: AI learns biases that exist in its training data.

check.q: What is the best way to verify a fact from a chatbot?
o: Ask a friend who agrees with you
Ask the chatbot if it is sure
Trust it if it sounds confident
Check it with two reliable sources
check.why: Cross-checking with reliable sources is the best test.

check.q: An AI gives you a link to a source. What should you do?
o: Trust it because it has a link
Open it and check it says what the AI claims
Copy it into your homework straight away
check.why: AI can invent links and sources, so open them.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by an AI hallucination.
practice.a: When a generative AI produces information that is false/made up (1) but presents it confidently as fact (1).

practice.q: An image generator mostly draws men when asked for "a pilot". Explain why this might happen and why it matters.
practice.a: The training data probably contained more images of male pilots/stereotypes (1), so the model learned that pattern (1); it matters because it is unfair/reinforces stereotypes or could discourage people (1).

pages.title: Using AI honestly
pages.spec: Use generative AI honestly in schoolwork and respect copyright and ownership
pages.summary: Using AI can be helpful or dishonest depending on how you use it and whether you say so. Passing AI work off as your own is plagiarism, and AI-made content raises questions about copyright and who owns what.
pages.starter: Is it cheating to use a calculator in a maths test? Is it cheating to use AI to write your English homework? What's the difference?
sc: I can tell the difference between using AI to learn and using it to cheat
I can acknowledge when I have used AI
I can explain copyright questions raised by AI-generated content

b: Using AI to explain, quiz you or give feedback can help you learn
Getting AI to do the work and handing it in as yours is plagiarism
Exams and coursework have strict rules: breaking them can mean losing marks or the whole qualification
When in doubt, ask your teacher and always say what you used
Acknowledge AI like any other source
Name the tool, the date, what you asked and how you used the answer
Example: "I used Copilot on 3 March to suggest ideas for my plan, then wrote it myself"
Your school's AI rules come first
AI is trained on work made by real artists, writers and musicians
Many creators say their work was used without permission or payment
Laws about AI and copyright are still being argued about in courts and governments
Never use AI to copy a real artist's style or voice and pretend it's theirs
slides.n: This is a live debate. Encourage pupils to see both sides: AI companies say training is like learning; many creators say it's copying.

blocks.text: Learning tool or cheating tool?

Generative AI can be a brilliant study partner: it can explain a topic in a different way, quiz you, or suggest how to improve a paragraph you wrote. But if you get an AI tool to **do** the work and hand it in as your own, that's **[[plagiarism]]**: presenting someone (or something) else's work as yours.

blocks.caption: Helpful or dishonest?
head: Use
Helpful or dishonest?
Why
rows: Ask AI to explain photosynthesis in simpler words
You are using it to understand
Ask AI to quiz you before a test
Ask AI to write your homework essay and hand it in
Ask AI for feedback on your own paragraph
Use AI in an exam or coursework when it's not allowed
It breaks the rules and can cost you the qualification

blocks.text: For GCSE and A level coursework, using AI without saying so can be treated as malpractice. You could lose your marks for that unit or the whole qualification.
Acknowledge it
If you do use AI (and your teacher allows it), **[[acknowledge]]** it, just like you would quote a book or website. Say which tool you used, when, what you asked it and how you used its answer.
Copyright and ownership
**[[copyright]]** is the legal right that protects people's creative work, like books, songs, photos and art. Generative AI raises big questions:

items: AI models were trained on millions of works by real people, often without asking them.
If an AI copies a real artist's style or voice, is that fair?
Who owns an AI-generated picture: you, the AI company, or nobody?

blocks.text: These questions are still being decided by courts and governments around the world, so the rules may change while you are at school.

blocks.title: Honest or not?
steps: Your group gets six scenario cards about pupils using AI.
Place each card on a line from "completely honest" to "cheating".
Agree a rule your class could use for using AI in homework.

q.q: Write your group's rule for using AI in homework.
q.a: Example: "You may use AI to explain, quiz or give feedback, but the final work must be written by you, and you must write a note saying which tool you used and how."

q.q: Choose the hardest scenario. Explain where you placed it and why.
q.a: A good answer explains both sides, e.g. "Using AI to fix spelling is mostly fine because the ideas are still yours, but if it rewrote whole sentences it becomes less your own work."

check.q: What is plagiarism?
o: Presenting someone else's work as your own
check.why: Plagiarism is passing off others' work as yours, including AI work.

check.q: Which use of AI is most likely to help you learn honestly?
o: Using it secretly in a test
Asking it to quiz you on a topic
Asking it to write your essay and handing it in
check.why: Quizzing yourself with AI supports your own learning.

check.q: What should you include when you acknowledge using AI?
o: The tool, date, what you asked and how you used it
Nothing, if the answer was good
check.why: Acknowledging means saying clearly how AI was used.

check.q: Why is copyright an issue for generative AI?
o: Models were trained on people's creative work, often without permission
AI work is always free to use
check.why: Creators argue their work was used without consent or payment.

practice.q: Give one way a pupil could use generative AI to help them learn, and one way that would be dishonest.
practice.a: Helpful: e.g. explaining a topic, quizzing, feedback on their own work (1); dishonest: e.g. getting it to write homework/coursework and handing it in as their own (1).

practice.q: "AI-generated art should belong to the person who wrote the prompt." Give one argument for and one against this view, and your conclusion.
practice.a: For: they came up with the idea/prompt and chose the result (1); against: the AI did the making and it learned from other artists' work/the company built the tool (1); a reasoned conclusion (1).

pages.title: AI, society and the future
pages.spec: Discuss the impact of generative AI on jobs, the environment and society, and form a reasoned opinion
pages.summary: Generative AI is changing work, learning and creativity. It brings opportunities and risks, including effects on jobs, energy and water use, and fairness, so societies are deciding how to regulate it.
pages.starter: Name one job you think AI will change a lot in the next ten years. Will it make the job better or worse?
sc: I can describe how generative AI may change jobs
I can explain the environmental cost of AI
I can give a reasoned opinion about a future AI issue

b: Some tasks will be automated: drafting, summarising, basic coding, translation
New jobs appear: AI trainers, AI safety testers, prompt designers, AI auditors
Many jobs change rather than vanish: people work with AI tools
Human skills matter more: creativity, judgement, care, teamwork
AI models are trained and run in huge data centres full of computers
These use a lot of electricity and water for cooling
Training one large model can use as much electricity as many homes use in a year
Choosing when AI is really needed is part of using it responsibly
slides.n: Link to the "Green computing" topic. Avoid quoting precise figures: estimates vary a lot and change quickly.

b: Governments are creating rules (regulation), e.g. the EU AI Act
Companies publish their own safety rules and test models before release
Schools and exam boards set rules for AI in learning
Your voice matters: you'll grow up with these tools

blocks.text: Work and jobs

**[[automation]]** is when machines or software do tasks that people used to do. Generative AI can automate tasks such as drafting emails, summarising reports, writing simple code and translating text. Some jobs will shrink, but new ones are appearing, and many jobs will **change** as people learn to work alongside AI. Skills that AI finds hard (creativity, judgement, empathy, teamwork and checking AI's work) become more valuable.
The environment

Generative AI runs in **[[data centre|data centres]]**: buildings filled with thousands of powerful computers. Training and using large models takes a lot of electricity, and data centres use large amounts of water for cooling. Every prompt has a small cost, and billions of prompts a day add up. Using AI when it's genuinely useful (not just for fun, a hundred times over) is part of being a responsible digital citizen.
Rules and regulation

**[[regulation]]** means official rules. The European Union's **AI Act** sorts AI systems by risk and bans some uses altogether. The UK has chosen to ask existing regulators to apply principles such as safety, fairness and transparency to AI in their own areas. AI companies also test their models for dangerous abilities before releasing them.

blocks.title: Opportunities and risks
items: Opportunities: faster learning, new kinds of creativity, help for people with disabilities, scientific discoveries
Risks: misinformation, unfairness and bias, job disruption, energy and water use, loss of skills if we rely on it too much

blocks.title: Class debate: "AI will do more good than harm"
steps: Your teacher splits the class into "for" and "against".
In your group, find three strong points with an example for each.
Debate! Each side gets two minutes, then one minute to respond.
Afterwards, write your own opinion, even if it differs from your side.

q.q: Write your best argument for your side, with an example.
q.a: For: e.g. AI helps doctors spot diseases earlier in scans, which saves lives. Against: e.g. AI-made fake news could damage trust in elections and real journalism.

q.q: Now write your own opinion in 3-4 sentences, giving reasons.
q.a: A balanced answer that weighs at least one benefit and one risk, gives a conclusion and explains it, e.g. "I think AI will do more good than harm if it is regulated, because…".

check.q: What is automation?
o: Machines or software doing tasks people used to do
check.why: Automation means tasks done by machines instead of people.

check.q: Why does generative AI have an environmental cost?
o: Data centres use a lot of electricity and water
AI uses paper to print answers
check.why: Running and training models takes energy and cooling.

check.q: What is regulation?
o: Official rules set to control something
check.why: Governments create regulation to control how AI is used.

check.q: Which skill is likely to become MORE important as AI improves?
check.why: Checking and judging AI output is a key human skill.

practice.q: Explain one way generative AI could change jobs.
practice.a: Some tasks will be automated, e.g. drafting/summarising (1); people will do new tasks/work alongside AI, or new jobs like AI auditors appear (1).

practice.q: "Schools should ban generative AI." Discuss. Give arguments for and against and a conclusion.
practice.a: For the ban: e.g. risk of cheating, misinformation, privacy (1-2); against: e.g. useful for learning, pupils need skills for the future, can't really be stopped (1-2); a reasoned conclusion (1). Max 4.

glossary.def: Computer systems that can do tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as recognising faces, understanding language or making predictions.
Artificial intelligence that creates new content such as text, images, audio, video or code.
The huge collection of examples (text, images, sounds) that an AI model learns patterns from.
The result of training an AI: a very large set of numbers that captures the patterns it has learned.
The instruction you give a generative AI tool, usually in everyday language.
A generative AI model trained on huge amounts of text that writes by predicting the next token.
A small chunk of text (a word or part of a word) that a language model reads and writes.
A program you can have a conversation with, often powered by a large language model.
The skill of writing prompts that get useful results from a generative AI tool.
Background information that helps an AI (or a person) understand what you need.
Repeating a cycle of trying, checking and improving.
When a generative AI states something false as if it were true, such as an invented fact or source.
When a system treats some people or ideas unfairly or one-sidedly, often because of patterns in its data.
To check that something is true, for example using reliable sources.
Presenting someone else's work (including work made by AI) as your own.
The legal right that protects creative work such as writing, music, photos and art from being copied without permission.
To say clearly where something came from, including which AI tool you used and how.
When machines or software do tasks that people used to do.
Official rules, for example laws that control how AI may be used.
A building full of computers (servers) that store data and run online services such as AI.
